articles.title: Man dies after car crashes into Wolverhampton Lidl
articles.summary: West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene with others requiring treatment.
articles.body:
A man in his 30s has died after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl shop in Wolverhampton.

Police were called to the supermarket in Finchfield Hill shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday.

West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and a number of other people were treated for injuries.

West Midlands Fire Service said it dispatched four crews to the incident at 17:51 BST with two crews still at the scene at 20:05 BST.

The car had crashed through the entrance of the shop, smashing the glass, and remained just inside the doors on Friday night as emergency services arrived at the scene.

Tina Bonev, who witnessed the crash, said it was "absolutely terrifying" and there had been "shock and confusion" in the aftermath.

Videos supplied to the BBC by eyewitnesses showed shoppers stood just metres from where the car had crashed into the store. Debris from the car and items from the shelves were strewn across the shop floor as an alarm sounded and a man shouted: "Everyone get out the store."

A woman could be heard asking: "Can anybody do first aid?"

Police have cordoned off Finchfield Road West and Finchfield Hill and a fire engine was parked outside the supermarket. Police said the roads were expected to remain closed for some time and advised drivers to find alternative routes.

Cars remained in the Lidl car park and the shop's entrance appeared to be damaged.

"The man's death is not being treated as suspicious and our thoughts are with his family at this sad time. Officers remain at the scene to help fire and ambulance colleagues carry out their enquiries," a police spokesperson said.

articles.title: In 2008, a North Dakota wheat farmer learned what lay beneath his fields: two oil wells on his land began sending him tens of thousands of dollars each month
articles.summary: Discover how John Bartelson, a North Dakota wheat farmer, turned his land's mineral rights into a lucrative source of income through oil royalties amid the Bakken oil boom.
articles.body: In North Dakota, a wheat farmer with the name of John Bartelson, started generating royalty payments because of two oil wells that were drilled on his land. The finances of farmers across the northern Great Plains were changing because of the oil boom in the Bakken formation, according to a June 2008 Bloomberg report. Bartelson, aged 65, was among the many landowners who started earning money from oil beneath fields that had, for a very long time, been used only to grow wheat.The two wells on Bartelson’s property were drilled by Houston-based EOG Resources Inc. in the previous year, and upon the arrival of his first royalty cheque, he said that he went into town for a beer. The money came from the oil that was being produced below the field, under an arrangement that permitted an energy company to drill while the person who owned the land received a cut of the revenue.Oil beneath the wheat fields drew new attentionThere was a growing interest in the Bakken formation, which is a large oil-bearing rock formation beneath parts of North Dakota, Montana and southern Canada. New drilling methods made it a lot more practical for companies to extract oil from rock that had once been difficult to develop, while rising oil prices also encouraged companies to invest in exploration and production.The state’s first major oil discovery came in 1951, when a well near Tioga struck oil in the Williston Basin. Production from early fields later declined, but companies began focusing on the Bakken, and interest returned. The State Historical Society of North Dakota states that there were renewed expectations for oil in 2007, and its history of the state’s oil industry describes how mineral rights and oil leases had been traded separately from the surface land for a very long time. It mattered to farmers because just owning the surface of a property did not always mean that they owned the mineral rights beneath it, but when a landowner held the relevant mineral interest and a producing well was drilled, the lease could provide royalty income.Royalty payments changed the economics of a farmA farm’s earnings usually depend on certain factors such as crop prices, yields, livestock and operating costs, and income from royalty became another source of money for landowners if their properties included oil reserves that were commercially productive. The amount that was paid could differ based on production, oil prices and the terms of the lease. Bartelson’s monthly payments were substantial, but they were kept specific to his wells and ownership arrangement, and were not a standard payment that was received by every farmer in the region.Drilling, equipment, services, transport and other work were paid for by oil companies, with North Dakota also collecting taxes and receiving revenue from mineral leases that were state-owned. It was estimated by a state economic report that private oil and gas royalties that were paid to North Dakota residents had managed to reach hundreds of millions of dollars in the mid-2000s, although those figures covered the wider industry.The boom brought opportunity, not a guaranteeThe Bakken boom opened up a new financial possibility for some rural landowners, but it goes without saying that the benefits depended on where the oil was located, who owned the mineral rights and whether it was commercially viable to drill. Recoverable oil was not found on every parcel, and not every landowner was entitled to royalties, while lease terms also affected the amount of money that reached the property owner.Bartelson’s experience was an example of a larger change in North Dakota, where advances in drilling technology and higher oil prices brought companies into areas that once upon a time had been known mainly for farming and ranching. Farmers used this opportunity since most of the land could continue to support agriculture at the surface and also produce oil below it.The change meant that mineral rights could become a valuable asset and could sometimes be worth more than the crops that are grown above them. As companies expanded across the Bakken, farmers such as Bartelson were learning how drastically their income could be affected because of the geology beneath their land.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight Ethiopia’s gov’t
articles.summary: Rebel commander pledged to continue fighting government-allied forces who seized Ethiopia’s Tigray capital.
articles.body:
An official in Tigray’s new federally backed administration has urged rebel forces to lay down their weapons in the northern Ethiopian region.

The call on Friday came hours after a rebel commander told his fighters to continue resisting government-backed forces despite losing control of Mekelle, the Tigray region’s capital.

Fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) were forced to withdraw from Mekelle in early October, after government-allied fighters entered the city to crush a rebel attempt to overthrow Ethiopia’s government.

Ethiopia’s government then installed a six-month caretaker administration in Tigray, promising to restore services, help displaced people return and prepare for elections.

But some fighting has continued, with Mekelle residents reporting a drone strike that killed four people and injured six others as they loaded goats onto a truck on Tuesday. The casualties could not be independently verified.

Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, a senior official in Tigray’s new caretaker administration, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to lay down their weapons.

“This is not the time for settling scores – I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,” he said in Mekelle.

He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city, maintaining the conflict served a small clique of leaders and not the people of Tigray.

Hours earlier, Lieutenant General Fisseha Kidanu, who was identified in a television broadcast as commander of the Tigray army, pledged to reverse recent military setbacks, saying Tigray was still at war.

“Local militias across the region – alongside all volunteers joining the resistance – are expected to engage the enemy,” he said Thursday on Tigray Broadcast Media, a new rebel television station. His location was not disclosed.

Fisseha urged attacks on government-held positions despite his opponents’ advantages in drones and heavy weapons. The TPLF has also claimed to have inflicted heavy losses on government forces. The Associated Press could not independently verify those claims.

The government’s allies include the Tigray Peace Force, comprising former members of the TPLF’s armed wing – a division within Tigrayan forces that has complicated the renewed conflict.

Redae said Ethiopian troops and allied forces were conducting joint security operations, including measures to prevent looting. He promised preparations for displaced residents to return but gave no timetable.

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, speaking Monday to the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, accused the TPLF of forcibly recruiting young people to fight instead of disarming under the terms of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement.

The renewed fighting has effectively shattered the agreement , which ended the region’s devastating 2020-2022 war.

That conflict caused an estimated 500,000 civilian deaths through violence, famine and collapsed health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium.

articles.title: In 2009, a South Dakota rancher bought a Powerball ticket on a feed run; days later, its numbers brought $232.1 million to a family whose home was repossessed
articles.summary: In 2009, Neal Wanless, a South Dakota rancher, won a record $232.1 million Powerball jackpot days after purchasing a ticket during a livestock feed run. This life-changing win came at a time when his family was facing financial struggles, including property tax debt and repossession. Wanless chose a cash payout of about $118 million, vowing to help those in need while continuing his ranching work.
articles.body: Neal Wanless bought a Powerball ticket at the age of 23, when he was living on his family’s ranch near Mission, South Dakota, during a trip to purchase livestock feed. He won a whopping $232.1 million jackpot on May 27, 2009, with the ticket matching all six numbers. He was supposed to claim the prize on June 5, at a time when his family had just lost a mobile home to repossession and was behind on property taxes.Wanless bought the ticket at an Ampride convenience store in Winner, which is a town that is located about 35 miles from the ranch. His family regularly made the trip to buy feed, and the $5 ticket was part of that routine, with the winning combination including numbers that were based on family members’ birthdays, according to the South Dakota Lottery’s announcement, which identified Wanless as the winner. The official lottery record lists the May 27 jackpot at an estimated $232 million, with a cash value of about $118 million.The family were unable to keep up with billsThe family lived on a ranch in an economically distressed part of South Dakota called Todd County, where they raised cattle, sheep and horses. The family was behind on property taxes, and a mobile home had been repossessed the previous year. They were described by the neighbours as hardworking people who had very little money to spare.Neal’s father, Arlen Wanless, used to buy and sell scrap metal to earn some money, but prices kept falling, which hurt that business. Friends and neighbours told the Associated Press that the family had faced financial hardship for years, and County records that were cited in the report showed that the family owed $3,552 in property taxes that were payable in 2007, 2008 and 2009.The news of the winning ticket quickly spread through the small community, and the convenience store that sold it was also due to receive a $50,000 bonus. For residents who knew the family, the win meant that the Wanlesses would no longer have to go through the same immediate financial pressure.He chose a cash payoutWanless claimed the prize at a ceremony in Pierre on June 5, where he chose a one-time cash payment instead of receiving the advertised jackpot in instalments. The cash option was worth about $118 million before taxes, and after federal tax withholding, the South Dakota Lottery said he would receive around $88.5 million. The important point to note is that lottery headlines usually feature the annuity value, which is paid over time, rather than the smaller lump-sum amount, and the $232.1 million figure was the jackpot that was advertised, not the amount deposited in Wanless’s account.Wanless spoke briefly at the ceremony and read a prepared statement, in which he thanked God for the opportunity and said he would not use the money recklessly. He also said that he wanted to help people in need, which pointed to the support that his own family had received from the community.He wanted to continue ranchingWanless said that he intended to continue working on the ranch even though the prize money was massive. He had been preparing to bale hay and carry out other farm jobs, and also spoke about buying a larger ranch, saying that he had told his horse, Eleanor, that they could go on longer rides if they had more land. Winning the lottery did not mean that he would leave his old life behind, as he had grown up around ranch work and wanted to remain involved in it; the money just gave him the option to expand the operation and help relatives and neighbours.Wanless’s win was one of the largest single-ticket Powerball jackpots at the time, and the story drew attention not only because of how large the amount was, but also because the ticket had been bought during an ordinary trip for feed, while the family was facing repossession and unpaid taxes. His public comments focused on continuing to ranch and repaying the community that had helped his family through hard times.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Read an excerpt from “Unthinkable” by Brandon Boudreaux
articles.summary: Read an excerpt from Brandon Boudreaux’s memoir: “Unthinkable: Lori Vallow Daybell’s Plot to Kill Me, and How Family, Faith, and Hope Saved Me”
articles.body: October 2nd, 2019, Gilbert, Arizona I buckled my four young children into their seats in my Tesla. I was in a rush to get them to the various places they needed to be that morning. As I started driving, my oldest son, age nine at the time, said our daily morning prayer. He prayed that I, his dad, would be safe while we were apart. The familiar prayer he had offered so many mornings that it had become as routine as the sound of the car starting. I barely heard him. My mind was on the gym and my business meeting later that morning. His prayer played underneath all of it, like the radio left on in the background of a drive. A couple of hours later, I turned onto my street alone, the kids’ car seats still in the backseat. Driving up the street toward my new house, I noticed a Jeep Wrangler with tinted windows parked in front, where my neighbor’s van usually sat. As I got ready to turn into my driveway, the Jeep’s rear window tilted up, just enough for what looked like something long and black to emerge. Crack! My driver’s side window shattered, but held in place. Before I could think, I slammed on the accelerator and my Tesla jumped forward. “Was that a gunshot? Did someone just shoot at me?” I sped past the Jeep, already reaching to dial 911. When I got to the end of the street, I looked over my shoulder and saw the Jeep make a U-turn and speed away. The next few hours were a blur. Police, shock, fear. Feeling faint as the adrenaline ran its course. I barely registered friends arriving. And going through my head, over and over: Someone just tried to kill me.

articles.title: After Operation Sindoor friction, Delhi & Baku reset ties with EAM Jaishankar's visit

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Amid ongoing efforts by both India and Azerbaijan for a reset in ties, EAM S Jaishankar and his counterpart Jeyhun Bayramov agreed to expand cooperation in energy, trade, investment and connectivity in a “very productive” meeting in Baku.Jaishankar’s visit to Azerbaijan was the first by an Indian foreign minister in eight years and built upon the diplomatic goodwill created by PM Modi’s meeting with Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev on the margins of the SCO summit in Bishkek last month.Ties between the two countries had been held back by geopolitical reasons for a while, mainly Azerbaijan’s ties with Pakistan — as evident from its support for Islamabad after Op Sindoor last year — and India’s defence ties with Armenia.While Bayramov spoke about taking the relationship to a higher level, setting aside past differences, Jaishankar underlined the significance of trade and energy cooperation. Terrorism was also among the issues discussed. “We spoke about economic cooperation, including trade, investment and energy, which are central to our bilateral ties... We believe there is very good scope for further enhancement of bilateral trade and investment. We also discussed various activities and exchanges,” said Jaishankar.“We spoke about connectivity because it is so important in a globalised economy,” he said, adding that they agreed to coordinate more closely on the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).The EAM also called on Aliyev in Baku. “Discussed strengthening relationship between our two countries. Appreciate his positive sentiments for this shared endeavour,” he said.Jaishankar welcomed peace agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia, expressing hope that it would lead to the establishment of a durable peace.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2026, researchers found Chicago’s St. Patrick’s dye peaked at 63 µg/L, neared background in days and stayed below levels predicted to harm river life
articles.summary: A recent study published in Environmental Science & Technology Letters found that the green dye used to color the Chicago River for St. Patrick’s Day peaked at 63 µg/L but posed a low ecological risk to aquatic life, according to researchers. The findings highlight the rapid decline of the dye's concentration and call for closer scrutiny of the annual event.
articles.body: The study was published on September 9, 2026, in Environmental Science & Technology Letters, where researchers identified the green dye as fluorescein, measured its concentration in the Chicago River after the annual St. Patrick’s Day celebration, and found that levels fell close to the river’s background level within a few days. The highest measured concentration was 63 ± 4 micrograms per litre, which was recorded within two hours of the dye being applied, and the authors said that the measured levels were well below concentrations that were predicted to cause harmful effects on aquatic life.The dye’s identity had remained a mysteryChicago has dyed its river green for St. Patrick’s Day since 1962, a tradition which began when city workers used dye to trace sources of pollution in the river. The event later became an annual celebration, with members of the Chicago Journeymen Plumbers Union spreading an orange powder that turns the water green.The exact formula was kept secret for decades, but in a 2025 report, Chemical & Engineering News noted that the dye was believed to be a fluorescein salt, but the ingredients had not been independently confirmed. The 2026 study provides direct chemical evidence that identifies fluorescein in water samples that were collected during the event.Researchers tracked how quickly the chemical disappearedThe team measured fluorescein concentrations after the dye entered the river and estimated an apparent attenuation half-life of about 15 hours, which means that the measured concentration declined through a combination of processes, including photochemical transformation. Within days, the readings were close to background concentrations.The authors compared the measured levels with predicted no-effect concentrations, which are estimates used to assess whether a chemical concentration is likely to harm aquatic organisms. The fluorescein concentrations that were measured were well below those thresholds, and the researchers came to the conclusion that the results indicated low ecological risk under the conditions they studied, which is not the same as proving that every possible effect on the river’s ecosystem has been ruled out.Why the river’s changing chemistry matters beyond the green colourThe 2026 study reported an apparent attenuation half-life of about 15 hours and found that the decline was consistent with photochemical transformation, which is a process in which light helps break down or alter a chemical. That matters because a substance’s concentration can fall as it transforms, while the resulting compounds may have different properties.The researchers’ measurements establish how fluorescein behaved in the Chicago River during the event they studied, instead of relying on the dye’s appearance as a measure of its persistence. Their findings also provide a starting point for further work on the environmental fate of the dye, and the study’s low-risk assessment applies to the concentrations that were measured and the ecological benchmarks that were used, and should not be interpreted as proof that every possible effect of repeated dye releases has been ruled out.Environmental groups still want oversightFriends of the Chicago River has argued that the event needs to be closely scrutinized as the amount of dye used has grown, and in a March 2026 statement, the organisation said that the green colour can remain visible for days and called for a review of whether the discharge should require a permit. It was concerned with the volume of dye released and the need to assess the river’s health. The new study adds chemical measurements to a debate that earlier relied heavily on claims about the dye’s safety, and its findings support a low-risk assessment for the fluorescein concentrations measured during the event, while leaving wider questions about repeated annual releases and the river’s full ecosystem outside the scope of that conclusion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
articles.summary: JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said. The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman. Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church. Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church. Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said. He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details. A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are underway at full speed.” Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra News Agency. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff. Jordan’s Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition. King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded.” Jordan’s Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism. Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman. Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.” Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism,” Hussein’s office said in a statement. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

articles.title: France on edge with 70,000 police deployed for unrest as authorities probe suspected terror attack near Paris
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron blames ultra-left groups for seditious acts as UNEF and Yellow Vest protesters vow to rally despite police rejecting permit requests.
articles.body: A suspected terrorist attack near Paris Friday added to tensions across France as the nation prepares for more potential violence Saturday. Seventy thousand law enforcement officers, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will be deployed across France as President Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to ward off another weekend of violent protests. "The strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by individuals or groups with no legitimate authority," Macron said ahead of the weekend after canceling his planned trip to Nigeria and Senegal originally scheduled for next week. "The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense," Macron added. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days." FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' "Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law," he added, "but alternative routes will be proposed" to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings. Adding to security concerns, a suspected terrorist attack occurred in the city of Trappes, west of Paris. A 39-year-old man was arrested by police after one person was killed and four others, including a 12-year-old girl, were wounded in what was originally said to be a "relatively random" shooting. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has since told local media, "The motive may be racist. The investigation is ongoing, but this is clearly a terrorist crime." The AFP reported the suspect appeared to fire randomly from a vehicle, and the mayor told reporters the dead victim and at least one of the wounded were "of African origin." Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal." FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS Ahead of Saturday's protests and after acknowledging that police had "lost control" during last weekend's unrest, Nuñez, the interior minister, said his ministry is "ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass." Reuters reports that the Union Nationale des Étudiants de France, or UNEF, one of the nation’s oldest student unions, has said its planned rallies will go on as scheduled despite police rejecting their permit requests. Police have so far only approved a union demonstration in Paris, Reuters reported, while denying requests from UNEF and the "Yellow Vest" movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018. Macron also took aim at those he says are behind the violence, saying, "Last Saturday, we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic." Earlier this week, Fabian Vanhemelryck, secretary general of the Alliance Police Nationale union, said political figures deserved blame because of "those who excuse the inexcusable, justify violence and prefer to overwrite police officers rather than condemn those who attack them." He also said the "state that abandons its police officers in the face of increasingly uninhibited violence, while demanding that they accept, remain(s) silent and continue(s) to hold the line." Major French institutions, like the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, will be closed in anticipation of Saturday’s planned protests, and 24 Metro stations across Paris will be closed. A Ligue 1 soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais, scheduled for Sunday night at Parc des Princes in the capital, has also been postponed to Monday evening. The NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints, scheduled for Sunday afternoon at Stade de France just north of central Paris, is still set to be played as scheduled, yet some weekend events around the game have been canceled. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Stade de France is the same stadium that hosted an international soccer match between France and neighboring Germany during the Nov. 13, 2015 terror attacks. Explosions were heard outside the stadium during the game that night, with then-French President François Hollande in attendance. Fans were held inside the stadium for hours while authorities dealt with the attacks unfolding around Paris that night. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Employee error blamed for toxic chemical leak that sent 60 people to hospital in Ohio
articles.summary: Some questions remain unanswered as the investigation continues, the mayor said
articles.body:
A chemical leak that sent 60 people to the hospital and forced hundreds of people to flee their homes has been blamed on an employee error.

Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz announced the cause of the tank leak at a news conference on Friday and said that all remaining evacuation orders in Toledo , Ohio .

The chemical leak happened Tuesday night when an employee of MC Tank Transport "introduced a temperature level to the tank in the process of trying to transfer the liquid" that caused a chemical reaction, the mayor said.

MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate , which it described as "an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better."

The evacuation orders were lifted after the company finished venting the tank that ruptured. That allowed a hazmat team to enter the site and test safety levels.

"At this time, we do feel confident that the site is safe," Toledo Fire and Rescue Battalion Chief Blake Molnar said.

Dr Brian Kaminski, vice president of medical affairs for ProMedica hospitals, said about 60 patients were treated at the hospital, most suffering relatively minor symptoms. A small number of patients who had underlying health conditions were admitted, he said, and all patients were expected to recover.

The company has "accepted responsibility" for what happened, the mayor said.

articles.title: Time ‘running out’ to reach Yemen’s Taiz amid deepening crisis, UN says
articles.summary: More than 800,000 people have been cut off from aid since the Houthis encircled Taiz city in early October.
articles.body:
A mounting humanitarian disaster is gripping Yemen’s Taiz after nearly three weeks of a Houthi siege that has prevented supplies from entering the city, the United Nations has warned.

The Iran-backed Houthis have encircled Taiz since early October, cutting off the road that links it to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Little fuel, food or other supplies have reached the city since.

“It’s 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off,” Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN’s humanitarian arm, OCHA, told a news conference in Geneva on Friday. “We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out.”

Most people depend on water brought in by trucks, the cost of which has tripled, Laerke said. Cooking gas is also “largely unavailable”, threatening community kitchens that provide meals to families.

Altogether, more than 800,000 people in Taiz are cut off from aid, about three-quarters of whom depend on humanitarian assistance, according to the UN World Food Programme (WFP). At least 200,000 are women and children.

While local humanitarian groups have been able to distribute their remaining supplies to keep water pumps and hospitals running, Laerke said, “It comes with a time code: The clock is running out.”

Fighting in Taiz province has intensified in recent days, with clashes reported in the Jabal Han highlands and the Dhubab and al-Masrakh districts.

Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for the forces of the internationally recognised government, said on Friday that troops had conducted raids and counterattacks in Taiz over the last 24 hours, “neutralising” 620 Houthi fighters and destroying 190 vehicles.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the figures.

Hospitals in the province are meanwhile reporting critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and supplies. Forty-two Taiz facilities face “acute” deficits, the World Health Organization spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.

The fighting has also deepened an ongoing hunger crisis. In Taiz alone, UN screenings have found more than 52,000 children to have acute malnutrition; approximately 11,500 are suffering from severe acute malnutrition.

“We’re desperately trying to regain access to Taiz, and we continue to support the broader operations across Yemen,” said Azfar Deen, a WFP regional communications officer for eastern and Southern Africa.

In response to the humanitarian fallout, the European Commission said on Friday that it would release an additional 22.5 million euros ($25.2m) in aid to Yemen, adding to the 87.5 million ($97.9m) previously allocated for 2026.

Yemen has been rocked by conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 to support the internationally recognised government.

A truce was brokered by the UN in 2022, but it fell apart this July, when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The ensuing escalation has displaced nearly 260,000 people, the majority in Taiz and Lahij provinces, according to the UN. More than 3,800 people have also fled to neighbouring Djibouti.

At least 1,574 people have been killed and 6,939 others wounded in the conflict since August.

articles.title: Argentina drops investigation into Milei over crypto fraud
articles.summary: Javier Milei had denied acting fraudulently when a cryptocurrency nosedived after he deleted a social media post about it.
articles.body:
A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.

The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.

The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.

He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.

Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.

Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.

The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.

But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.

It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.

The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'.

The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly.

Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".

And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

articles.title: Irish politicians disavow ‘demeaning’ PSA warning grandparents not to hug family without asking consent
articles.summary: A viral ad in Ireland warning against grandparents hugging grandchildren without asking for consent sparked outrage and was pulled by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre.
articles.body: An ad released by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) in Ireland that urged grandparents to ask for consent before hugging their grandchildren sparked international controversy after it began airing last month and has since been removed. In September, an ad from the DRCC’s We-Consent campaign went viral for showing grandparents greeting their grandchildren. One grandchild appears receptive to a hug, while the other does not. A narrator says, "Not everyone wants a hug, even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely." The ad has since been removed and criticized by politicians from multiple parties in Ireland. The BBC reported that Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan of the Fianna Fáil party, whose department funded the campaign, announced the video has been removed after discussion with the DRCC, and declared, it "does not represent the views of the Government." IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND 'NOT OVERRUN' BY MIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS "It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them," O'Callaghan said. "While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive." Irish Sen. Gareth Scahill of the Fine Gael party blasted the video as a waste of public funds. "What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which, at best, has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," Scahill said. "The issue of consent is a very serious one, and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children. "But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark." TRUMP SAYS HE WOULD 'LOVE' TO SEE IRELAND UNIFIED AS ONE NATION Scahill also asked, "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?" The DRCC told Irish broadcaster RTE in a statement, "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland. "We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too," the organization added. "We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have." "Instead of honestly acknowledging what is behind the doubling of rape rates from a decade ago, which is who the government chooses to let into the country, these institutions lecture grandparents about hugging their grandkids, as though that has any remotest connection to the problem at hand," she said. In 2024, The Irish Independent reported that reports of sexual assault had nearly doubled in Ireland between 2012 and 2022. articles.summary: Cameron Diaz bought the Hollywood Hills home in 2004, but she never lived in it. She kept it as a buffer property beside her own residence.
articles.body: Cameron Diaz bought the Hollywood Hills home in 2004, but she never lived in it. She kept it as a buffer property beside her own residence. Nearly two decades later, Ariana Grande bought the house for $4.9 million in an off-market deal, adding another property to her growing real estate portfolio, ABC reported.A Hollywood Hills home with Sunset Strip viewsBuilt in 1950, the mid-century home sits at the end of a small cul-de-sac, with breathtaking views of Los Angeles’ famous Sunset Strip. The home spans 1,800 sq. ft. and has two bedrooms and two-and-a-half bathrooms. It sits on half an acre of land, much of which is steep hillside. The tall black gate, hedges and trees give the house the privacy its famous owners seek. Privacy is a major highlight, especially in a neighbourhood filled with stars.As the house was never publicly listed for sale, few details about its interior are available. Tax records, however, provide some insight into its size and mid-century origins.Cameron Diaz never lived in the houseCameron Diaz purchased the property in 2004 for $1.8 million. Rather than using it as her primary residence, she kept it as a ‘buffer’ between her neighbouring property and the surrounding area, according to a report by Dirt. She had bigger plans for the house. City records from 2009 show plans to tear it down and replace it with a much larger residence, the housing tracker reported. However, those plans never progressed beyond the planning stage. As the house remained standing, it underwent a series of renovations over the years.In 2018, Diaz updated the house with a new roof and windows. She also expanded the kitchen, remodelled the two bathrooms and added a powder room. She retained the original details while updating the property with modern conveniences. By the time Grande purchased it, the house had already benefited from these improvements. The renovations left the home in working condition, although it has no pool.A quiet saleAriana Grande bought the house in 2022 for $4.9 million, AD reported. However, the home was never listed for sale. The transaction never reached the open market, so little information about it was available to the public before the deal closed. Reports put the price at $4.9 million, nearly triple what Diaz had paid 18 years earlier. However, details of the interior and other amenities remain private. Tax records describe a single-storey, mid-century layout.The property added to Grande’s collection of homes in California. She had already established a substantial real estate portfolio, with properties in the Los Angeles area and beyond. At the time of the purchase, Grande was living in another Hollywood Hills residence in the Bird Streets neighbourhood. She had also sold a separate property in the Hollywood Hills in autumn 2021. articles.title: Tennessee woman challenged her brother’s deed giving their nephew his home after his death; appeals court restores the clause letting him inherit it all
articles.summary: A homeowner living with Alzheimer's disease signed a deed giving his nephew survivorship rights to his home, and his sister, who held his power of
articles.body: A homeowner living with Alzheimer's disease signed a deed giving his nephew survivorship rights to his home, and his sister, who held his power of attorney, sued to undo it. After a trial and an appeal, the Tennessee Court of Appeals decided the deed stands as written. When a family member with a serious illness changes who inherits his house, relatives sometimes fight over whether the decision was truly his own. A Tennessee case shows how courts weigh that question. Here’s what happened, how the judges analysed mental capacity and undue influence, and why the survivorship language mattered.How a Tennessee homeowner with Alzheimer's disease came to sign a deed sharing his house with a nephewAccording to the written opinion of the Tennessee Court of Appeals, published by Justia, the homeowner was Marshall Ricker, an architect who needed extensive daily care as he aged, first from his sister, Linda Ricker. Her son, Clark Blumenstein, lived in Washington state. In January 2019, Marshall Ricker emailed his nephew's father, asking that the nephew move to Tennessee, live with him, help him and receive $2,000 a month. He named his sister sole heir and executrix in his will that April and gave her power of attorney that September. On March 13, 2020, with a notary present at his nursing home and the nephew on the telephone from Washington, he signed a deed making himself and his nephew joint owners with survivorship rights, so the survivor takes the whole home. He died on July 4, 2020.Why an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis alone did not prove the homeowner lacked mental capacity to signLinda Ricker's argument was that her brother could not have understood what he signed. The nursing home records supported her, describing disorientation, poor judgment, rambling thoughts and inappropriate behaviour, including a March 11, 2020 note that he appeared to be worsening. Judge Kristi Davis, writing for the three-judge panel, answered that an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis does not automatically make someone incapable of conducting a transaction. The question is whether the person understood the nature, extent, character and effect of the transaction when it happened, and the challenger bears the burden of proof. Linda Ricker told the trial court she could hold intelligent conversations with her brother in March 2020, and Clark Blumenstein testified that his uncle knew what he was doing. Because the trial judge heard both witnesses in person, the appeals court deferred and affirmed.Why the sister's claims of undue influence and a confidential relationship failed against the nephewLinda Ricker argued that her son had effectively become her brother's caregiver, creating a confidential relationship and a presumption of undue influence. In Tennessee, such a relationship, followed by a benefit to the dominant person, can shift the burden to that person to prove fairness by clear and convincing evidence. The trial court found that Linda Ricker, not her son, was the caregiver, and the appeals court found the record supported that conclusion, noting she held her brother's power of attorney and led his care. Helping a relative carry out his wishes, the judges wrote, does not automatically turn an ordinary family relationship into a confidential one. Blumenstein testified that the move and the deed were his uncle's purposeful, independent decisions and that he facilitated rather than controlled them. The panel affirmed the finding of no undue influence.Why the appeals court restored the survivorship language that the trial court had struck from the deedThe most consequential part of the ruling concerned a single clause. After trial, the Greene County Chancery Court concluded the deed was valid but struck the survivorship language, reasoning that such a deed is technical and that the homeowner appeared to have had no independent legal advice. That would have left the nephew with a half share and sent the other half to Linda Ricker under her brother's will. On August 10, 2026, the Tennessee Court of Appeals modified that part of the decision. Neither side had asked for the deed to be reformed, the trial court made no finding of mutual mistake, and, having found that the homeowner understood the transaction and entered it freely, there was no basis for parsing his grasp of individual clauses. The deed must be enforced as written, the court held.How the mortgage payoff, the withdrawn money and the Tennessee Adult Protection Act claim were resolvedLinda Ricker also challenged other financial decisions. She alleged that Blumenstein wheeled her brother into a bank on February 13, 2020, where he paid off a mortgage of roughly $185,000, and pointed to $27,000 Blumenstein withdrew from his uncle's funds in late June 2020. Blumenstein told the trial court the payoff was his uncle's way of ending ties with a former wife and that the withdrawal reimbursed moving costs. The trial court found the payoff proper and treated $12,000 as part of an exchange for his move from Washington. Because it found no exploitative acts, both courts rejected her claim under the Tennessee Adult Protection Act, which sought compensatory damages, punitive damages and attorney's fees. Judge Davis wrote that the evidence did not undercut the trial court's findings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Deciding with fake images: More candidates are using AI in political ads to get your vote
articles.summary: At least 220 ads— mostly Republican— generated or enhanced with artificial intelligence have circulated in the leadup to the midterms, at a cost of almost $137 million.
articles.body: South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette appears distressed in a gloomy room as she undergoes a polygraph test that ends with the lie detector catching fire. Although the video clarifies that the “dramatizations” in this political ad are generated with artificial intelligence, some voters still asked her whether what they saw was real, Evette told Noticias Telemundo. At first, Evette said she thought, “This is ridiculous, right? Like, nobody could possibly believe this?” Later, as she traveled the state during her campaign to become the Republican gubernatorial nominee — a race she lost in June to Attorney General Alan Wilson — she said she encountered voters who were confused about the video’s veracity. “On the campaign trail, I would have people ask me, like, ‘Oh my gosh, did they really make you take a lie-detector test?’” Evette said. She then had to explain to them that it never happened and it was an AI-generated fake ad. “So you almost think it’s a joke and you kind of laugh at it, until you realize that there is a group of people out there that can’t tell the difference,” she said, “and then start to question if what they’re saying may be true.” Evette is not the only one whose image was manipulated in the lead-up to the midterm elections. The Wesleyan Media Project, a group of experts that tracks political propaganda in campaigns, identified at least 220 ads produced or enhanced with artificial intelligence by candidates or political action committees this election cycle. They cost just under $137 million. It’s a significant leap in the use of this technology compared to 2024, when the investment in AI was less than $50,000 during the presidential election. As of May of this year, the money spent on these AI ads was already $20 million. “We really saw the growth in AI ads over the summer,” Travis Ridout, a professor at Washington State University and one of the project directors, told Noticias Telemundo. “A lot of them were connected with closely fought primary races.” The lieutenant governor of South Carolina saw two videos of herself generated with artificial intelligence, or deepfakes, but she also shared one that falsely depicted her opponent, Alan Wilson, rejecting a call from President Donald Trump. According to Evette, her campaign used artificial intelligence after the ads featuring her circulated. “But we said it, ‘This ad is AI-generated,’” she said. The videos targeting Evette are said to have been paid for by a PAC; the one released against her opponent was funded by the lieutenant governor’s campaign. A request for comment sent to Wilson was not immediately returned. In response to a query from Noticias Telemundo on social media, nearly 40 people said they had seen political ads generated with artificial intelligence. Some admitted that they have difficulty distinguishing them. “And that could be deceptive; voters could be basing their decisions on falsehoods in that case,” Ridout said. “That’s, I think, what’s most concerning from a democratic perspective.” In the absence of a federal law regulating them, the responsibility falls to local governments, said Ridout, who estimates that about 30 states have some type of rule or requirement regarding AI in political campaigns. Of the 220 ads analyzed by the Wesleyan Media Project, only 27% revealed they used artificial intelligence tools. The possibilities ‘are endless’ Candidates with smaller campaign budgets rely on artificial intelligence to compete with their rivals, Ridout suggested. “I think it’s here to stay. I don’t know that it’s going to go away,” said Evette. Campaigns “are extremely expensive,” she noted, and AI reduces many recording and editing costs. These tools could also “unlock” more creativity in political advertising, said Ridout, “which wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world.” He said the possibilities are practically endless and include satire. Among the ads he analyzed, he saw candidates emerging from a swamp, boxing against Trump, or appearing alongside physicist Albert Einstein, who died in 1955. “I do worry about the lasting impact of those images, even if people know that it might not be true,” Ridout said. He noted those images might stick in their mind when they’re voting, or it may even generate waves of misinformation that trigger violence. AI can “redefine” modern political campaigns, the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonprofit institute whose experts have analyzed the potential impact of this technology on democracy, said in an article. Mekela Panditharatne, legal adviser and director of the center’s Elections and Government Program, said that without disclosure, “generative AI use in political ads has the potential to distort perceptions of candidates, painting candidates in a flattering light or their opponents in a negative light.” During the Minnesota primaries, a deepfake circulated showing Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, smiling amid mountains of money. A spokesperson from her office said that although it didn’t stop them from winning the primary, there was alarm over the impact of the AI-generated video. “There is already too much distrust in our politics, and voters deserve to know what’s real and what’s not,” the spokesperson said. Minnesota is one of the states with AI regulations; in 2023, its Legislature passed with bipartisan support a ban on its use to influence elections. The AI ad targeting Flanagan elicited debate over whether it was unlawful or whether it was protected under the First Amendment. Artificial intelligence “should never be used to manipulate voters,” Flanagan’s spokesperson stated. A matter of transparency At least two federal bills to regulate AI in politics are pending discussion and approval by lawmakers. One seeks to ensure that advertisements have conspicuous notices that artificial intelligence tools have been used; the other attempts to prohibit this technology “to generate materially deceptive content falsely depicting federal candidates in political ads to influence federal elections.” Although local regulations exist, some candidates still violate them, according to Panditharatne from the Brennan Center. “I think those laws have not had as strong a deterrent effect as we would like,” she said, making a point for the need of a universal federal standard. When designing any law, legislators take into account the First Amendment, which protects, among other rights, freedom of speech, religion and the press. Laws that are “carefully tailored” could withstand scrutiny under the First Amendment, Panditharatne explained. AI can also be used to create “forms of commentary or art,” such as parodies or satire. In the ads analyzed by Noticias Telemundo, the form and content indicating it was done with AI varied; there were differences ranging from the text size to the wording. One, for example, stated, “This ad contains digitally generated content,” while another referred to it as “dramatizations.” In some, the warning appeared at the end, and in others, it was omitted altogether. The use of AI in political propaganda concerns both Democrats and Republicans, according to Ridout. Candidates from both parties have been targeted by deepfakes, “and they don’t like that.” He thinks next year there could be consensus in Congress to impose some national standards. Republicans use more AI Republican-backed PACs and GOP candidates appear more willing to invest in these tools than Democrats and independents, according to a review by the Wesleyan Media Project. It found that 81% of the 220 ads identified were funded by Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups. Another 12% were from pro-Democrat sponsors. The remaining ads were sponsored by independent candidates or groups weighing in on issues that were not ostensibly partisan. Although Ridout said he has no explanation for this marked difference, he believes the key may lie in each party’s voters. Democratic voters, he said, tend to be “more in favor” of government regulation and perhaps Democrats may be more constrained by their own voters in terms of what they are willing to do, as opposed to Republicans. If a candidate “goes too far” in an ad against their opponent, they may also face backlash and criticism, he said. However, he noted that PACs, which typically fund their own ads, have less accountability to the public, “and I think they might be more likely to cross some lines,” he added. In some of the advertisements during this election cycle, AI was used for aesthetic enhancements, such as improving image quality or dramatizing events in the candidate’s life. But in others, it was used to criticize candidates by falsely portraying them alongside immigrants, trans people or drag queens as these groups have become greater targets. “That’s worrying,” Ridout said. There are also political figures or people who appear more frequently in AI ads; Trump’s image is often artificially used to suggest that he supports or endorses a candidate. New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is “a favorite among Republican advertisers,” the study found. AOC appeared in at least five altered videos that were negative portrayals. Noticias Telemundo requested comment from her office but has not yet received a response. The states that used AI the most in political campaigns were Oklahoma and Texas, the Wesleyan Media Project found. ‘Very dishonest’ In Louisiana, the Republican Senate primaries heated up after the release of AI-generated videos pitting Rep. Julia Letlow against State Treasurer John Fleming. Fleming said he saw between five and six videos with his AI-generated image and believed that they influenced Letlow’s victory. In one ad, reviewed by Noticias Telemundo, Fleming appears driving a bus with a Mexican flag, falsely suggesting that he was transporting immigrants from the southern border to U.S. territory. Fleming denounced the ads as “highly dishonest” and deceptive, as they showed him endorsing policies that he has never supported. They were also designed “to make you look unattractive physically,” he said. Although he acknowledged that those aspiring to public office are exposed to criticism and scrutiny — and that lies are also spread without AI — he insisted that political ads must be based on “truths.” His constituents were “very upset” about the videos, Fleming said, and although he said he tried to convince them that they were fake, “when you are outspent by a ratio of 20 to one, your voice is not heard.” In an interview with a local station, Letlow distanced herself from the AI ads targeting Fleming, claiming they were from PACs with which she had no connection and indicated that she was “not a fan” of AI in political campaigns. She also criticized Fleming for sharing on his social media an AI-generated video of herself in which she can be heard talking about her husband, Luke Letlow, who died from Covid complications days before he was to take office as a representative of Louisiana’s 5th Congressional District. Letlow now occupies that seat after a special election. Letlow has said that Fleming “crossed the line” with the AI-generated ad. “Releasing this video is shameful and indefensible. The family is off-limits, period,” she said. Her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When asked about the video, Fleming said that “the ad was from someone else, and all I did was post it temporarily, but it was actually very accurate.” Other Republican figures in the state asked Fleming to remove it. Ultimately, the person who created it was the one who deleted it, according to Fleming. Deny, deny, deny Given the growing popularity of artificial intelligence in the political arena, candidates will have to dedicate increasing amounts of time to debunk AI-generated advertisements circulating against them, according to Ridout. This is especially true as the technology advances to the point where it becomes more difficult to distinguish what is real, and people doubt everything they see. Both Evette in South Carolina and Fleming in Louisiana said it’s necessary to have safeguards to distinguish and clearly mark this content. “I don’t think that AI is the issue per se,” said Fleming, who mentioned that there were ads generated with this tool that supported his campaign using humor. “I think it’s whether you use AI in a productive and positive and truthful way.” Doubting some candidates is not “intrinsically bad,” Panditharatne of the Brennan Justice Center said, but the issue is the corrosive effect of distrusting electoral processes or institutions. Another risk to democracy, Panditharatne pointed out, is that some politicians will dismiss truths in what is known as the liar’s dividend. This means “disregarding or rejecting credible and authentic evidence by attempting to discredit it as false or AI-generated.” To combat that, digital literacy initiatives are necessary to encourage voters to carefully analyze what they consume without denying the reality of everything they see, Panditharatne said, since “that’s not healthy either.” An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

articles.summary: FC Twente fans have made regular pilgrimages to Stranraer after a friendship formed by a terminally-ill supporter and two visiting Scots.
articles.body:
Dennis Van Unen's dying wish was to experience an Old Firm match in person.

The FC Twente fan, who had terminal cancer, achieved that dream in 2006 with the help of two Stranraer supporters.

What followed was an unlikely friendship between fans of the Dutch club and the Scottish town that has endured ever since.

That bond has now been immortalised in fabric through a special tartan-inspired shirt, which will make its debut in FC Twente's Dutch Eredivisie match away to AZ Alkmaar this weekend.

The unlikely connection began in 2006 when Dennis met Stranraer supporters Jim McKie and James Hilton during a match at Twente's De Grolsch Veste stadium, in the eastern city of Enschede.

Suffering from skin cancer, Dennis told them his dream was to experience one of football's most intense rivalries, a match between Celtic and Rangers.

Jim, who also supported Rangers, and James, who was a Celtic fan, secured tickets and accompanied him on a football tour that included Ibrox, Celtic Park and Hampden.

The friendship formed during that visit survived Dennis's death the following year, with Twente supporters subsequently travelling to Stranraer and establishing a tradition of reciprocal visits that continues to this day.

The first outing of the new tartan strip will be keenly watched more than 400 miles away from the match, at The Grapes pub which is home of the Stranraer Tukkers.

The supporters' group takes its name from the nickname given to people from the Twente region.

The bar is barely a long clearance from Stranraer FC's Stair Park, but the walls outside are adorned with the Saxon Steed which features on the Twente badge, while inside, the club's traditional red and white colours greet visitors.

Landlord Billy Hodge, 70, found himself as the unlikely model for the club's marketing campaign, filmed around the town two weeks before the shirt went on sale.

"It was strange to be honest, I never fancied myself as a model," he told BBC Scotland News.

"I knew there was something secretive going on when they contacted me, but I didn't expect this. The kit is fantastic."

Before Dennis died at the age of 34, Jim and James travelled to Enschede, near the German border, to say a final farewell to their friend.

The visits continued after his death, with supporters from Twente and Stranraer making regular trips in both directions as the friendship between the two groups grew.

The links between the clubs were enough for Twente to travel to Stranraer for a pre-season match in 2017 , marking 10 years since Dennis' death.

Billy remains a Twente season ticket holder and travels to matches a couple of times a season, where he and the Stranraer contingent are often welcomed into the club's hardcore section with open arms.

"When they come over, we'll get them a beer on the house, it's the same over there," he said.

"We do get a lot of tourists down this area and if they are Dutch, they know the horse that's on the front of the pub. We had a couple of guys cycled over. They got the ferry to Newcastle and then took all the back roads."

Billy added: "I think the two sets of fans are similar. They are all working class guys, they back their team through thick and thin and I think they are to be applauded for that".

Twente's Scottish links extend back further than Dennis' initial trip.

The club sported a similar tartan away shirt in the 1994/1995 season, later voted their best ever by fans.

Former Motherwell defender Rob McKinnon spent two years at Twente between 1996 and 1998, while striker and current Aberdeen Women boss Scott Booth won the Dutch Cup with the side in 2001.

The side have not lifted the Eredivisie since 2010, when they were under the management of Steve – or should that be "Shteve" – McClaren who was ribbed for adopting a strange accent during his time at the club.

However, they are competing in the Europa Conference League this season and sit fifth in the Dutch top flight after nine games.

Leon Molenkamp, the club's marketing manager, said the shirt had already been a hit with supporters.

He said it was a way to ensure the "unique" relationship was not forgotten by future generations.

"The relationship is very heartfelt," he said.

"We have people visiting back and forward multiple time a year. It is great to see how something like that can just arise.

"It's getting to be quite a well-known friendship with fans in Twente as well and more and more people are going over and taking an interest in Scottish football."
