articles.title: Colorado high school volleyball players faced alleged benching threat amid trans athlete dispute
articles.summary: Two Colorado high school volleyball players were allegedly threatened with benching after discussing a transgender athlete in their program.
articles.body: Two Colorado high school volleyball players were threatened with benching after discussing a transgender athlete in their program, according to a parent complaint alleging the girls were ultimately allowed to play on condition they stop discussing the issue. The school district that oversees the school, Jefferson County Schools, is currently under Title IX investigation by the U.S. Department of Education. A screenshot of an email, obtained by OutKick, from Dakota Ridge High School's head volleyball coach to a parent says the parent's daughter would miss a match over reports of alleged bullying. The screenshot does not identify the actual words that were used. "Over the past several days, we have received multiple reports alleging that your daughter used language toward teammates that could be characterized as bullying," the message bearing the coach's name states. "As a result, your daughter will not be eligible to participate in today’s match." EX-SJSU VOLLEYBALL COACH FILES NEW LAWSUIT ALLEGING RETALIATION FOR TRUMP SUPPORT, RELIGION AMID TRANS SCANDAL The message says the volleyball program emphasizes character, respect and how players treat one another, describing the reported behavior as falling short of its standards. It offers to discuss the matter with the parent after the match. Meanwhile, Tanna Donalson, whose daughter was cut from the program in August, wrote in an Oct. 6 email to district that her daughter had reported two varsity players were told they would be benched after discussing the situation among friends. Donalson said she was subsequently informed that, after the players’ parents met with the coach and the athletic director, the girls were permitted to play on condition they not discuss the issue again. The email was seen by OutKick in a copy of a Title IX complaint Donalson submitted to the Education Department. "[The daughter] reported that Mr. Zeman pulled three varsity volleyball players aside and told two of them they would be benched for today’s game because they had discussed this issue amongst themselves. According to the account relayed to me, four friends had been discussing privately what they had learned, and one reported the conversation to a teacher. I was further informed that, after the two players’ parents met with the athletic director and Mr. Zeman, the players were permitted to play on the condition that they not discuss the issue again," Donalson wrote. "Please determine what was said, the basis for the proposed benching, and whether participation was conditioned on refraining from discussion of or support for our complaint." Lindsay Datko, founder of the parent advocacy group Jeffco Kids First, also said she had reviewed emails concerning the threatened discipline. "We have seen emails showing that girls were threatened to be benched because they were expressing their frustration in a very adolescent manner," Datko told OutKick. But Datko added the coach backed away from the threatened benching. EDUCATION DEPARTMENT RESCINDS BIDEN TITLE IX RULE, RESTORES TRUMP-ERA REGULATIONS Jeffco Chief Legal Counsel Julie Tolleson acknowledged Donalson’s report in an Oct. 6 email response. "She can include these matters in her review, though we won’t be able to discuss with you any disciplinary or other action involving any other student," Tolleson wrote, referring to the district’s Title IX coordinator. A day earlier, Tolleson had instructed Donalson to report any retaliation or harassment related to her complaint. "District policy prohibits retaliation," she wrote. In response to OutKick, Jeffco defended its policies and cited student privacy restrictions. Its statement did not address the alleged condition on the players’ participation or explain what remarks prompted the proposed discipline. The school district provided the following response in full: "We recognize that fairness in athletics, student safety, privacy, and equitable opportunities for students are important issues for our community. "In accordance with Colorado state law (including the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act), Jeffco Public Schools is committed to providing a safe, welcoming, and inclusive environment for all students. Jeffco’s policies ensure that every student, regardless of gender identity or expression, has equal access to educational programs, facilities, and district-sanctioned activities. "High School Athletics: Jeffco Public Schools operates high school athletic programs under the governing bylaws of the Colorado High School Activities Association (CHSAA) and Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act. "District Policies on Equal Educational Opportunities Jeffco Public Schools' nondiscrimination policies—including Policy AC (Nondiscrimination/Equal Opportunity) and related guidance—remain fully active and in effect. "Under federal law (FERPA) and state privacy regulations, Jeffco Public Schools cannot confirm, deny, or comment on the gender identity, administrative records, or athletic participation of any individual student. "We are navigating a complex national climate, but our local commitment remains steady: all students deserve to feel safe, respected, and supported in Jeffco Public Schools. We support and value all members of our Jeffco community, including our transgender students and staff members. "Jeffco Public Schools is committed to cultivating environments where all students, staff, families, and members of our community are accepted, respected, and feel that their voices and perspectives are valued. While people may have differing views on Jeffco policies and the laws that inform them, we all share a responsibility to ensure our words and actions reflect care and respect for others. We ask everyone in our community to respect individual privacy and remember that real children and families are at the heart of these conversations. "Jeffco will continue to follow all state laws and regulations with respect to our schools, athletic programs, and students’ rights. Our responsibility - and steadfast commitment - remains to serve every student and ensure that our schools are places where all students can learn, grow, and thrive." Donalson’s own complaint centers on the roster decision that ended her daughter's junior-year school volleyball season. Her daughter, 17, had played in the program during her freshman and sophomore years. Her mother said coaches encouraged the setter to learn right-side hitting before ultimately cutting her. In an Aug. 13 email, the coach said the change was intended to give her daughter another opportunity to demonstrate her skills. He said other athletes showed greater consistency in setting, defense, serving, decision-making and other areas, and described the roster decisions as a collective coaching evaluation. WASHINGTON STATE'S HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS LEAGUE PUTS ONUS FOR TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY ON STATE LAWS "She competed for a spot, other athletes ultimately demonstrated more consistency in the areas needed, and she was beat out," he wrote. The coach is also her daughter's history teacher. Correspondence documents Donalson’s request for a different placement and the school’s offer of a teacher change for second semester. Donalson responded that she wanted to give the situation a few weeks before deciding. She explicitly told school officials she was not alleging that classroom retaliation had occurred. Asked whether her family had experienced retaliation since speaking publicly, she said she had reported that some students made comments to her daughter, but their family had received substantially more support than opposition. "We have received far more support than we have anything opposite of that," she said. The U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights issued findings March 13 that the district violated Title IX through its policies on girls’ athletics and access to female facilities and overnight accommodations. OCR issued a notice of impending enforcement action June 26. Jeffco disputes those findings. The district sued Education Secretary Linda McMahon and the Education Department on July 28, challenging the enforcement actions and arguing that the federal demands conflict with Colorado law and threaten its funding. That lawsuit concerns the district’s broader policies, rather than a determination about Donalson's daughter's roster decision. Colorado voters will consider Proposition 134 on Nov. 3. The measure would require school-based teams to be designated for biological males, biological females or mixed participation, with eligibility tied to those categories and an exception allowing females to join male teams when no equivalent female team is offered. "I am not against the trans community or any community for that matter," Donalson said when asked about the measure. For Donalson and her daughter, she says the impact of the situation has been "deep and wide," and has jeopardized her daughter's dreams of playing in college. "She still has those dreams, it's a little difficult to figure out how we're going to achieve them, as this is her junior year, and arguably her most important year, because that is when you start communicating with coaches," Donalson said. "And right now we have nothing to share." She said her daughter still plans to play club volleyball and pursue college opportunities. But losing her school season has affected how she experiences the sport. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Every time she plays, she just remembers all that’s transpired here, and it just has taken a little bit of the joy of the sport out of it for her," Donalson said.

articles.title: At 19, Chloë Grace Moretz bought a Spanish-style Los Angeles home for $3.4 million in 2016; seven years later, the half-acre estate, with an updated kitchen, sold for $5.65 million, $2.25 million above its purchase price
articles.summary: Chloë Grace Moretz was only 19 when she bought her first house in Los Angeles. She was already working in films.
articles.body: Chloë Grace Moretz was only 19 when she bought her first house in Los Angeles. She was already working in films. In 2016, she paid $3.4 million for a Spanish-style home in Studio City, according to a report by Realtor.com. Before that, Moretz and her parents had rented a place in Bel-Air. So this purchase marked her move from renting to owning.A house built for hostingThe house sits on about half an acre. Spanning roughly 6,700 square feet, it has a double-height great room with a fireplace that anchors the main floor. Designed with entertaining in mind, the house also has a den, a theatre and five bedrooms, giving family and friends plenty of room to spread out. “The master suite is a true oasis, complete with a sitting area, fireplace, dual walk-in closets, and an oversized bathroom with a jacuzzi tub,” the Redfin listing said. The bedrooms get plenty of natural light and feature soaring ceilings and custom details throughout. The sellers updated the kitchen before the sale. It has a large island, a breakfast nook and high-end appliances.The outdoor space is equally exceptional. There is a patio, a living area with a fireplace and an outdoor kitchen beside a pool and spa. The house also has a separate studio with its own kitchenette, giving guests a place of their own. The garage can accommodate several cars, and there is additional parking in the walled courtyard.Chloë Grace Moretz lived in the home for seven years. In February 2023, she listed the property for almost $6 million, with an asking price of about $5.995 million. The sale closed in March 2023 at $5.65 million, slightly below the asking price.The $5.65 million sale price may look like a win because it was $2.25 million more than she paid. From that perspective, the increase was about 66 per cent. However, this figure does not account for estate agent fees, closing costs or renovation expenses.Studio City has long attracted high-profile buyers and sellers. In December 2025, Olivia Wilde sold her sprawling Studio City home for $5.23 million. Interestingly, the sale came amid speculation about her romance with British art dealer Caspar Jopling. She bought the house in March 2023 for $5.9 million and listed it for $6.2 million two years later. The property was described as “an exceptionally private modern-ranch retreat” in the Redfin listing. “Sunswept is at once private, pedigreed, and deeply livable – an extraordinary creative compound designed for both entertaining and everyday life, just moments from Erewhon, Equinox, and the best Ventura Boulevard has to offer,” the listing says.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Cuba next? Trump hints at 'little stopover' after US warships return from Iran war
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has revived his threat of intervention in Cuba, suggesting that American warships returning from the war with Iran could stop
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has revived his threat of intervention in Cuba, suggesting that American warships returning from the war with Iran could stop near the island before secretary of state Marco Rubio steps in to negotiate a deal.Speaking at a rally in South Florida on Friday, Trump responded to a question shouted by someone in the crowd about Cuba. His remarks came just days before the US midterm elections, with voters concerned about rising prices of essentials, including fuel and groceries, amid the war with Iran.“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”Trump had floated a similar idea earlier this year but had not raised it publicly in recent months. He has repeatedly suggested that Cuba could become the next focus of US intervention after the Iran war, which he has long predicted would wind down but has not yet ended.Trump and Rubio turn up pressure on CubaTrump and Rubio have both adopted a hard line towards Cuba's communist government. In May, the two renewed the possibility of US military intervention, with the threat gaining further significance after the Trump administration announced criminal charges against former Cuban leader Raúl Castro.Trump told reporters in the Oval Office at the time that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades, adding that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”Rubio has argued that Cuba poses a national security threat because of its relationships with countries hostile to the US. Although he has said Washington wants to resolve its differences with Havana peacefully, he has expressed doubts about reaching a diplomatic agreement with the island's current leadership.Shortly after Trump's speech on Friday, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba. Addressing those seeking to bring about change on the island, he urged them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”Rubio has not spoken extensively about Cuba in recent weeks. In a September 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, he described the island's economic and political situation in stark terms.“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without referring to any CIA operation.“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”Talks continue as Washington tightens sanctionsDespite the increasingly tough rhetoric, US and Cuban officials have held meetings in recent months to explore ways to improve relations. Trump administration officials, including Rubio, have taken part in discussions with Cuban representatives.However, the US side has emerged dissatisfied with the talks, leading Washington to impose further sanctions on the Cuban government.Addressing the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”. He added that he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”A few days later, Trump said he expected the two countries “will make a deal”, adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”The two countries also clashed at the United Nations earlier this week after the Trump administration sought to rally opposition to an annual resolution condemning Washington's decades-old economic embargo against Havana.Cuba faces a deepening economic crisisCuba has been struggling with a severe economic and energy crisis since 2020. Its economy has contracted, while its population of around 10 million has faced widespread power cuts, food shortages and rising prices.The crisis has also triggered repeated waves of public protests and a significant exodus of Cubans, with hundreds of thousands leaving the country, many heading to the United States.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas family bought more than 3,000 acres along the Rio Grande and gave 586.9 acres to the state for just $1; the land became a state park
articles.summary: Along the Rio Grande in southern Texas, a family bought more than 3,000 acres of land in the late 1930s, as an old settlement in the area faded into
articles.body: Along the Rio Grande in southern Texas, a family bought more than 3,000 acres of land in the late 1930s, as an old settlement in the area faded into history. Much of the property was developed, but a stretch of woodland known for its Texas ebony trees was kept intact. As reported by Texas Parks & Wildlife, in 1944, the Bentsen family transferred 586.9 acres to the state for just $1, under an agreement that the land would be used for a public park. The gift laid the groundwork for Bentsen–Rio Grande Valley State Park, which opened in 1962, preserving part of the valley’s distinctive landscape.Bentsen–Rio Grande Valley State Park traces its roots to Spanish land grantsLong before the Bentsen family acquired the property, the land formed part of a much older pattern of settlement along the Rio Grande. Spanish settlers arrived in the area during the 1740s. In 1767, colonial authorities distributed large parcels through a system of land grants known as porciones, which were assigned to individuals.The ground occupied by the present-day state park was once included in Porcion 50, associated with José Antonio Zamora. Over the following decades, the original grants were divided into smaller holdings, and settlements developed along the river. The landscape was not untouched wilderness, even then. People had lived and worked on the land for generations, and the history of ownership stretched back well before the modern Texas border took shape.How the Bentsen family preserved the Texas ebony woodlandOne of the small communities that emerged in the area was called Las Nuevas. By the late 1930s, however, the settlement had been abandoned. As reported, around that time, the Bentsen family purchased more than 3,000 acres from land that had once formed part of the original Spanish grant.The family went on to develop more than 2,000 acres north of the land that now makes up the state park. A separate portion was left undeveloped because of its stands of Texas ebony trees, which helped distinguish the property from the surrounding landscape. Those trees became a defining feature of the land the family would eventually place in public ownership.The decision meant that a section of the former land grant would not follow the same path as the family's developed holdings. The woodland remained in place, preserving an area of the Rio Grande Valley's natural landscape.Bentsen family donated 586.9 acres under a public park agreementIn 1944, the Bentsen family donated 586.9 acres of the former Porcion 50 to the Texas Parks Board. The stated payment was just $1, an amount recorded in the agreement transferring the land to the state.The arrangement came with a specific condition. The property had to be used for public park purposes and maintained and identified as Bentsen Rio Grande Valley State Park. It was not simply a transfer of acreage without restrictions; the contract established the intended public use of the land.The donation took place nearly two decades before the park opened. In the intervening years, the land remained set aside for the purpose specified in the agreement, while the family’s wider holdings had already undergone development.How the $1 land transfer led to Bentsen–Rio Grande Valley State ParkBentsen–Rio Grande Valley State Park officially opened in 1962, giving the preserved woodland a permanent place within Texas's state park system. Located a few miles southwest of Mission, the park occupies part of a landscape shaped by centuries of settlement, land division and changing patterns of ownership.Its origins are unusual in one particular respect: the state received the land for a nominal sum, but the transfer was made with a clear commitment about how it should be used. The 586.9 acres had been retained from a much larger family purchase, and their preservation helped establish the public park that exists today.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spread
articles.summary: The Ebola outbreak has now spread to four countries across eastern, central ⁠⁠and western Africa.
articles.body:
Kenya has announced its second Ebola death, as the virus outbreak spreads from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to several parts of Africa.

The Kenyan Ministry of Health said on Friday that the latest death was that of a 65-year-old woman who had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died ⁠⁠of Ebola earlier this month.

The ministry added that Kenya currently has seven Ebola cases receiving treatment at two isolation facilities.

All the cases are within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”, it added.

Kenya’s first Ebola case was identified this month in a man who travelled from DRC to Kenya and died at ‌‌a Nairobi hospital on October 5.

Since then, Kenyan authorities have traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine, with nine cases confirmed, including the two patients who died.

The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths. The deadly disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.

The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central ⁠⁠and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

On Tuesday, Nigeria became the fourth ⁠⁠African country to report an Ebola case. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad ⁠⁠Ali Pate said on Friday that an analysis showed the case was closely ‌‌related to the virus detected in the index case ⁠⁠in Kenya.

Uganda announced on Saturday that travellers ⁠⁠with a history of ⁠⁠travel to DRC would not be permitted to transit through the East African ⁠⁠nation.

Uganda had recorded 20 people infected, almost all of whom had travelled from DRC, and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors, episode eight: Series left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
articles.summary: A newly earned special power left one contestant with a powerful decision to make in Friday's episode.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife.

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried. "Oh bottoms!

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor - one that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson".

"Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.

Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six , said she was now praying that the heat on her would go away.

While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".

Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however.

"This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast.

"We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."

Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed.

"But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, "OG traits", still flying it up."

After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."

He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."

With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool , Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something.

"How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh.

"It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.

Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".

On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows.

"This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."

The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.

Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold.

"I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.

But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.

Things got tense when Sharon, by her own later admission, "got mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.

In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny.

"I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."

The special power was revealed to be a double dagger, enabling one of "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to have two votes at the night's roundtable.

King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade.

"I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor.

"I feel like whoever it is, they are five sets ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"

Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.

With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.

As discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!"

Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael.

"If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.

Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."

In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.

Kenny bought it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" looking tantrum in the task earlier on.

Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round.

"Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon.

"I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."

The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.

Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes.

With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

articles.summary: LeBron James was caught practicing his golf swing during the national anthem before his 76ers debut, prompting Trump to call it a "TOTAL DISGRACE."
articles.body: NBA star LeBron James was shown practicing his golf swing during the playing of the United States national anthem before his 76ers debut on Tuesday. Later in the week, President Donald Trump called James' conduct a "TOTAL DISGRACE" on social media. The story itself is quite simple. James practiced his golf swing during "The Star-Spangled Banner." Trump criticized him for it. And yet, the headline writers at ESPN apparently didn't see it quite as clearly. According to ESPN.com on Thursday, "Trump criticizes LeBron James for not standing still during the national anthem." Take a look: Here's the full clip of James during the national anthem: Describing what James did as merely "not standing still" is an awfully charitable characterization. He wasn't shifting his feet or adjusting his uniform. He was practicing his golf swing while the national anthem played. The framing minimizes the conduct at the center of the controversy. ESPN suggested James' behavior was innocuous and Trump's criticism was excessive. That was the point. ESPN must feel it has an obligation to protect James. The headline writers must have also agreed James was wrong. Otherwise, there would be no reason to sanitize it as James merely failing to "stand still." At least athletes who kneel during the anthem generally claim that they are doing so as a form of protest. James offered no such explanation. He simply sought to make a mockery of the anthem. It also wasn't the first time. James was caught practicing his swing during the national anthem on Christmas Day last year. There’s something cringe about a star American athlete who previously criticized NBA executive Daryl Morey for supporting Hong Kong protesters now behaving this way during the U.S. national anthem. At this stage of his career, the NBA also has to ask how much James still benefits its brand. James turns 42 in December. He has averaged 15 points per game through his first two games this season and, unsurprisingly at his age, is a shell of his former self.
